segments.text: The ETO gives legal recognition to electronic records and transactions so that a transaction is not rejected merely because it is in electronic form.

Prepare how electronic writing/signatures can satisfy legal-form requirements, attribution and acknowledgement of electronic records, dispatch/receipt, certification-service providers and offences affecting digital trust.
Primary authority: Electronic Transactions Ordinance, 2002, read with current evidence/cybercrime law where relevant.

The Electronic Transactions Ordinance, 2002 gives legal recognition to electronic records and transactions so that a transaction is not denied effect merely because information is in electronic form. Its logic is functional equivalence: electronic methods can satisfy legal requirements of writing, signature, original form or retention when the statutory conditions are met.
This does not mean every digital message automatically proves a contract. Formation, attribution, authenticity and evidentiary reliability still have to be established under the relevant law.

Electronic signatures connect a person with an electronic document or transaction through a recognized method. The legal strength of a signature depends on the statutory scheme, reliability of the method and the surrounding evidence. Certification service providers can support trust in digital authentication.

Electronic records also raise questions of time and place of dispatch and receipt, retention, integrity and attribution. These rules matter because online transactions often cross physical and jurisdictional boundaries.

The Ordinance contains rules with extra-territorial significance and provisions addressing misuse connected with electronic transactions. Students should read these together with later cybercrime legislation where a contemporary offence question goes beyond the Ordinance itself.

In litigation, electronic material must also satisfy evidence law. Legal recognition of an electronic document and proof that a particular electronic record is authentic are related but separate issues.

items.text: The basic policy is technology neutrality:
a legally relevant transaction should not fail merely because information or a signature exists in electronic rather than paper form, provided statutory requirements are met.
Legal recognition of electronic writing and signature comes first. Then study attribution: how an electronic record is linked to a particular person or system.
Acknowledgement confirms receipt or processing; dispatch and receipt rules help determine when and where an electronic communication is legally treated as sent or received.
Certification-service concepts support trust in electronic authentication, while offence provisions protect the integrity of electronic transactions and certification processes.

rows: Common confusion to avoid: Do not describe an electronic signature as simply typing a name. The statute defines legally recognized methods and conditions for authentication.

items.text: Study legal recognition before technical details.
Prepare attribution, acknowledgement, dispatch and receipt as a sequence.
Use exact statutory language for digital/electronic signature concepts.

segments.text: Electronic form can have legal effect when statutory requirements are met.
Authentication links an electronic act to a person or system.
The Ordinance also creates offences relating to misuse and false certification.
